claims.text: The starting material is a self-lubricating high-entropy alloy in the FeNiCrCoCu system.
The untreated alloy initially has a homogeneous elemental distribution and no intentionally segregated surface phase.
Post-fabrication annealing at 600–700 K under an inert atmosphere will induce preferential copper surface segregation in FeNiCrCoCu.
The annealing treatment will form a continuous, nanometer-scale, copper-enriched surface layer.
The copper-enriched surface layer will be thin and coherent.
Moderate-temperature annealing increases the mobility of copper atoms.
Copper has relatively lower surface energy, which promotes its segregation to the alloy surface.
Surface-segregated copper atoms assemble into a coherent, low-shear layer.
The Cu-rich surface film acts as an in-situ solid lubricant by lowering interfacial shear strength during sliding.
Lowering interfacial shear strength through the Cu-rich film reduces both coefficient of friction and wear rate.
The annealed alloy will show approximately 20–30% lower coefficient of friction than the untreated alloy under identical loading and temperature conditions.
The annealed alloy will show approximately 20–30% lower wear rate than the untreated alloy under identical loading and temperature conditions.
The lubricating benefit should persist in sliding tests from approximately 300 K to 900 K.
The untreated alloy has higher friction and wear at elevated temperatures because of its homogeneous elemental distribution and temperature-induced lattice disorder.
The beneficial effect will diminish when the service temperature exceeds the stability range of the Cu-rich film and causes oxidation or melting.
Insufficiently controlled annealing will fail to produce selective copper segregation and a continuous lubricious layer.
The expected quantitative improvement may vary with processing parameters, alloy microstructure, and test conditions.

The hypothesis is falsified if annealed specimens fail to achieve a statistically significant reduction greater than 15% in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the tested temperature range, or if a Cu-rich surface layer cannot be detected.
